new_statements.rule_in_words: Pévé is described as a three-tone language (H, M, L; lexical tone plus grammatical H tone for perfective). Stress is mentioned only as a non-contrastive factor that can perturb perceived tone; the grammar (as far as every indexed passage shows, and per Lovestrand's review of its thin phonology chapter) gives no rule for where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author flags tonal variation and possible toneless grammatical particles as needing further research (p.50, p.53).
new_statements.domain_note: Remarks concern surface tone of morphemes/clause-final particles in connected speech; no word-level stress domain is defined. Text obtained only as verbatim Google Books search snippets (saved), not from a held copy of the book.
new_statements.identity_note: Shay 2019 describes Pévé as spoken around the Chad-Cameroon border (data from one speaker, Lazare Wambadang, elicited in Maroua) = peve1243 proper. Sachnine 1982 describes Lamé / vùn dzèpàò of Cameroon, which Glottolog lists as dialect lame1268 under peve1243 but which Shryock 1997 (p.33) classes as the southernmost dialect of Heɗe (herd1234-type, ISO hed); WALS 'Lamé' [lam] and UPSID/PHOIBLE 'LAME' are built on Sachnine. Venberg 1975 describes Peve of Chad (Lutheran Brethren mission area).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pévé is a three-tone language (high, mid, low); every vowel carries a tone and tone is both lexical and, on verbs, grammatical (relative high tone = perfective). Stress is mentioned only as a phonetic/discourse-level factor ('stress and intonation patterns') that can perturb or even supersede surface tone, and the grammar states explicitly that such changes are not contrastive. No word-stress placement rule is given anywhere in the 384 pages, stress is never marked in transcriptions, and there is no stress or accent section.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated about stress. The author notes (pp. 50, 52-53) that surface tone varies with intonation, stress patterns, neighboring tones, vowel quality and discourse factors, that linguist and native speaker sometimes perceive tone differently, and that the tonal analysis 'calls for further research'. Also p. 11: surface tone 'may be affected by intonation and stress patterns, which themselves may be affected by context, previous discourse, the speaker's motivation, and other factors.'
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the Pévé dialect proper as spoken by co-author Lazare Wambadang, born 1968 in the Pévé village of Bad dis Sem (Badissem), northern Cameroon, just west of the Chad border (p. 9), with data from 2012 fieldwork in Cameroon. Wambadang treats Pévé, Dari and Doué as mutually comprehensible dialects differing mainly in tone (p. 3); Herdé and Dzəbao are viewed by him as pidgin varieties with Mesmé. Sachnine's 'Lamé (Vún Dzəbao)' is identified with the Dzəbao variety, not Pévé proper (pp. 1-3), so Sachnine 1982 (not among the open works) should not be read as describing this same variety without a caveat.
